# Esukārī Sutta (MN 96 (PTS MN ii 177))

**ID:** MN 96 (PTS MN ii 177)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Esukārī Sutta* (MN 96) is the ninety-sixth discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya*, set at Sāvatthi in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Monastery [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The dialogue occurs between the Buddha and the brahmin householder Esukāri, who approaches the Buddha to defend the brahminical view of social hierarchy and privilege [Dutt; McTighe; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Esukāri propounds that birth determines social division, positing four grades of service—whereby a brahmin can be served by all four classes, a kshatriya by three, a vaiśya by two, and a śūdra solely by another śūdra—alongside four corresponding types of hereditary wealth [Thomas 1933; Hazra 1994; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The Buddha counters that one's true worth depends on conduct rather than caste [SuttaCentral; Hazra 1994]. He teaches that service should be evaluated purely on ethical and spiritual outcomes: one ought to serve someone only if such service increases faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom [Thomas 1933; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Furthermore, he identifies the noble Dhamma as a person's true wealth [McTighe]. Using the simile of kindling fire, the Buddha explains that just as fire ignited from different types of wood possesses the same heat, flame, and brightness, members of any caste who go forth are equally capable of accomplishing the wholesome Dhamma [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Priestley 1999]. Convinced, Esukāri declares himself a lay follower [Dutt; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995].

A full parallel to the sutta exists in the Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* at MĀ 150 [SuttaCentral], located in fascicle 37 of Taishō 26, which DharmaNexus aligns across 24 matching passages [DharmaNexus]. Anesaki notes that the Chinese counterpart is longer and includes a shepherd simile absent from the Pali recension [Anesaki 1908]. DharmaNexus identifies extensive internal Pali reuse across 99 texts, including prominent overlaps with other discourses on caste such as the *Assalāyana Sutta* (MN 93, §16.1–16.12) and the *Subha Sutta* (MN 99), as well as doctrinal parallels in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (AN 10, AN 3, AN 4) and the *Puggalapaññatti* [DharmaNexus]. Additional cross-language textual alignments appear in the Tibetan *Vinayavastu* and Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu* [DharmaNexus].
